Confidence Intervals for a Fit

Source: R/inference.R
confint.StatmodFit.Rd

Returns confidence intervals for the coefficients of every distribution parameter, by default the Wald ones and otherwise by inverting a likelihood test.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'StatmodFit'
confint(
  object,
  parm = NULL,
  level = 0.95,
  vcov_type = bayesian_vcov(),
  readable = TRUE,
  test = wald_test(),
  interval = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

object

A StatmodFit().

parm

Which coefficients: a distribution parameter's name, a term's name, a vector of parameter:coefficient labels, or NULL for all of them. With readable = TRUE, the name of a quantity is accepted as well.

level

The confidence level.

vcov_type

A vcov_method object, passed to vcov.StatmodFit(): bayesian_vcov() (the default), frequentist_vcov() or unconditional_vcov(). The conventions are compared at vcov_method.

readable

Whether to report the quantities in which the model is written (a term's own parameters under the names of the literature) and not the raw coordinates. The value is passed to vcov.StatmodFit() and must be FALSE for a restricted test (test_restricted()).

test

A test_statistic object, the test whose acceptance region is the interval. wald_test() (the default) gives the interval that is symmetric about the estimate, from the variance matrix and with no refit. lr_test(), score_test() and gradient_test() are inverted by statmod_invert() and cost a few dozen restricted refits per interval. For the position of a break-point of a modelterms7::seg() term, a limit that the data do not bound (the statistic is under its critical value at the end of the range of the variable) is -Inf or Inf. The four are compared at test_statistic.

interval

NULL (the default), which inverts test, or a bootstrap_interval object, percentile_interval() or basic_interval(), whose limits are quantiles of the bootstrap replicates stored in the fit. The standard error is then the bootstrap one, and vcov_type and a test other than wald_test() are rejected.

...

Passed to vcov.StatmodFit(), which signals an error for any argument that it does not take.

Value

A data frame with the parameter, the term, the coefficient, the estimate, its standard error and the two limits.

Details

With readable = FALSE, the interval for a coefficient of a linear predictor is symmetric about the estimate and needs no mapping back. Such a coefficient is unbounded whatever the distribution parameter to which it belongs, because the link has already carried that parameter onto the whole line, so the scale on which the interval is built is the scale on which the quantity lives. The interval does not respect a bound on the distribution parameter itself; for that, map an interval for the predictor through the inverse link at the covariate values of interest. With the default readable = TRUE, each quantity that a structural term declares (a loading or a persistence, for example) has an interval built on the link scale of that quantity and mapped back, so that interval is not symmetric.

The variance comes from vcov.StatmodFit(), so the same three conventions apply, and a coefficient that a kinked penalty has set to zero has NA in place of an interval. For an interval around a penalized term, vcov_type = unconditional_vcov() does not treat the smoothing parameter as known.

Inverting a test instead

The argument test takes a test_statistic object (see there for the four statistics) and selects the statistic whose acceptance region is the interval. The Wald interval is the set of \(b\) that the Wald statistic does not reject, and it is symmetric by construction: that statistic is a parabola in \(b\), since the curvature is read once at \(\hat\beta\). The other three read the likelihood at each \(b\) in turn, so their intervals follow its shape and are not symmetric where it is not. Where the likelihood is nearly quadratic the four intervals agree; with a small sample and a skewed likelihood the likelihood-ratio and gradient intervals shift away from the Wald interval.

Each of the three is found by statmod_invert(), which brackets the crossing outward from the Wald interval and locates it with a root finder, so one interval requires a few dozen restricted refits. The parm argument therefore selects the coefficients before the search and not after it, so that only the requested intervals are computed.

A row for which the restricted fit is not defined keeps NA limits. testable_coords() identifies those rows: a coefficient under a kinked penalty, an aliased one, and every coefficient of a model carrying a structural term. The estimate and the standard error in such a row are those of the fit and do not depend on test.

A coefficient under a penalty that is twice differentiable (a smooth's own coordinates, a ridge, a random effect) is inverted like any other, and the interval is the credible one that vcov.StatmodFit() gives for it under vcov_type = bayesian_vcov(), conditional on the hyperparameters that the fit reached. See statmod_stat_at().

The three restricted tests (lr_test(), score_test() and gradient_test(), the ones for which test_restricted() is TRUE) need readable = FALSE, since a test is about one coefficient and a readable quantity is a function of several at once.

See also

vcov.StatmodFit(), summary.StatmodFit(), test_statistic, vcov_method, statmod_test(), which tests one coefficient against a value of its own, and statmod_invert() and statmod_stat_at(), the two internal functions from which an inverted interval is built

Examples

set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = runif(80))
dd$y <- 1 + 2 * dd$x + rnorm(80, sd = 0.4)
fit <- statmod(y ~ x, distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd)
confint(fit)
#>                   parameter   term coefficient  estimate         se      lower
#> mu:(Intercept)           mu linpar (Intercept)  1.043291 0.08770104  0.8714004
#> mu:x                     mu linpar           x  2.007856 0.14865515  1.7164973
#> sigma:(Intercept)     sigma linpar (Intercept) -1.032801 0.08006408 -1.1897235
#>                        upper
#> mu:(Intercept)     1.2151822
#> mu:x               2.2992148
#> sigma:(Intercept) -0.8758781
confint(fit, "sigma")
#>                   parameter   term coefficient  estimate         se     lower
#> sigma:(Intercept)     sigma linpar (Intercept) -1.032801 0.08006408 -1.189723
#>                        upper
#> sigma:(Intercept) -0.8758781
confint(fit, parm = "mu:x", test = lr_test(), readable = FALSE)
#>      parameter   term coefficient estimate        se    lower    upper
#> mu:x        mu linpar           x 2.007856 0.1486552 1.716674 2.299038
